Students will explain the impact of word choice using the frame 'The phrase ___ suggests ___, which creates a mood of ___.'"},{"kind":"foundational-skills","text":"Students will add today's vocabulary words to their Unit Vocabulary graphic organizers. Students will examine r-controlled vowels (hazards, eternal) and the suffixes in wickedly and wistfully to support accurate decoding and spelling."}],"essentialQuestions":["How does the 'apathy' of the Fields of Asphodel represent a different kind of danger than a monster?"],"connections":{"knowledgeBuilding":"Students have followed Percy into the Underworld and seen how Riordan blends ancient Greek myth with modern life. Today they study how modern comparisons make the ancient idea of the afterlife feel familiar and unsettling.","enduringUnderstanding":"Authors choose figurative and connotative language on purpose. Modern metaphors can carry ancient ideas about morality, and a danger does not have to look like a monster to be frightening.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 28, students will return to Chapter 19 (pp. 310–319) to cite Hades's accusations and Percy's responses. not caring","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"judgement","definition":"a decision about whether someone or something is good or bad, right or wrong","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"symbolic","definition":"standing for or representing a larger idea","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"figurative","definition":"using words in a non-literal way, such as metaphor or simile, to create a picture or idea","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"hazards","definition":"dangers or risks","tier":"support"},{"word":"wickedly","definition":"in an evil or very mischievous way","tier":"support"},{"word":"stalactites","definition":"icicle-shaped rock formations that hang from the ceiling of a cave","tier":"support"},{"word":"connotation","definition":"the feeling or association a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Book 1)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 300–309 (Chapter 19)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate the idea that danger can take forms other than monsters and connect it to the Underworld setting they are about to reread.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"Dangers Without Fangs","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn and talk with your partner. Be ready to share one idea with the class."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"So far, Percy has fought a Fury, a Minotaur, and a Hydra. Today we read about a place with no monsters at all, but it may be just as dangerous."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Besides a monster, what is something that could be dangerous to a person's life or spirit?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Boredom or not caring could be dangerous. If you stop trying or stop caring about anything, you can waste your whole life. A monster is scary because you can see it, but giving up is quieter."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Hold onto that idea. Today we will see how Riordan uses comparisons and carefully chosen words to make a quiet danger feel real."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Take two or three shares, and listen for the words 'not caring', 'giving up', or 'stuck'. Sound-spelling and suffix practice: hazards, eternal (r-controlled vowels); wickedly, wistfully (suffix -ly)."},{"type":"directions","text":"Open your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. Add each word as we discuss it. Write a student-friendly definition in your own words and a quick sketch or example."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let's start with sound patterns. Say *hazards* and *eternal* with me. Notice the *ar* in haz-ards and the *er* in e-ter-nal. When a vowel is followed by *r*, the sound changes. It is neither a short nor a long vowel. Underline the r-controlled vowels in each word and read them again."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Now look at *wickedly* and *wistfully*. Both end in *-ly*, a suffix that turns a describing word into one that tells how something is done. Wicked plus -ly means in a wicked way. Wistful plus -ly means in a wistful way. Circle the suffix in each word."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"The word *apathy* begins with *a-*, which can mean 'without,' and *path* comes from a Greek word meaning 'feeling.' What do you think *apathy* means?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It means without feeling, like not caring about anything. Someone with apathy doesn't get excited or upset about stuff."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"*Eternal* comes from a Latin root meaning 'age' or 'time.' How does that help you with the meaning, and what word do you know that is related to it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It has to do with time that doesn't end, so eternal means lasting forever. Eternity is related. Maybe it's like the word *eternally*."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Two more connections. *Symbolic* comes from *symbol*, something that stands for a bigger idea, like a dove standing for peace. *Figurative* comes from *figure*, as in a figure of speech. Figurative language is not meant literally. When Riordan compares one thing to another, he is being figurative, and the comparison is often symbolic of a bigger idea."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"*Charisma* and *tragic* both describe people or events. Which one would you use for a very charming leader, and which for a very sad ending?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Charisma is for the charming leader, like someone everyone wants to follow. Tragic is for the sad ending, like when something terrible happens and could not be fixed."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"*Wistfully* means with sad longing. *Judgement* is a decision about whether someone was good or bad. Keep both in mind. We will see souls who wait wistfully and who are sorted by judgement."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Keep this brisk, about one minute per cluster. Students will use the words again in Learning in Action. Make sure every student has all eight words in the organizer before moving on. Accept either spelling of judgement/judgment if students use the other; the text uses the Outline's spelling."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: hearing and spelling r-controlled vowels or the -ly suffix","tryThis":"Have students tap and say each syllable (haz-ards, e-ter-nal, wist-ful-ly), underline the r-controlled vowel, and circle -ly. Then have them write each word twice from memory."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: using word parts to infer meaning","tryThis":"Ask students to find two other words with the root path (sympathy, empathy) or the prefix a- (atypical, amoral) and explain how the word parts help define each. Have them compare apathy and empathy."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students reread the Fields of Asphodel passage to interpret figurative language and cite evidence. Part B: Students distinguish connotations and write an explanation of how word choice creates mood and shows a different kind of danger.","activities":[{"id":"lia-close-read-figurative","title":"Part A: Interpret the Figurative Language","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Close Read & Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 19","pages":"pp. 300–309"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the description of the Fields of Asphodel in Chapter 19. Using a two-column chart, record each figurative phrase in the first column (for example, the souls waiting for a concert that will never start, and the stalactites compared to booster rockets). In the second column, write what the comparison means and what feeling it creates. Underline words that show how the souls act or feel."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A literal description tells us what is there. A figurative description helps us feel it. Riordan could have said 'souls wandered the plain.' Instead he compares the scene to something modern, like a concert crowd. As you read, ask two questions: what two things are being compared, and what feeling comes with that comparison?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the comparison to a concert that will never start tell us about the souls in the Fields of Asphodel?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It shows the souls are waiting around for something exciting that is never going to happen. At a concert people are excited at first, but if it never starts they just stand there bored and stuck. That fits the souls who aren't being punished or rewarded, just waiting forever."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Riordan compares the stalactites to booster rockets. Why would he use a modern, high-tech image in an ancient place?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It makes the Underworld easier to picture because I know what booster rockets look like. It also makes the place seem odd, like old rock turned into machinery, which is a little unsettling. Riordan keeps mixing the old myth with the modern world."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What mood do these phrases create together? Which words from the text help you decide?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The mood is hollow and gloomy, like nothing matters. Words like 'never start' and the way the souls just drift and wait make it feel empty and endless. Nobody is happy or sad, just numb."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4"],"stem":"Why does Riordan compare the souls in the Fields of Asphodel to people waiting for a concert that will never start?","choices":[{"text":"To show that the souls are excited about something that will happen soon","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses the start of the comparison, people waiting for a concert, with its meaning. The concert never starts, so the excitement never pays off."},{"text":"To show that the souls are stuck in endless, empty waiting with nothing to look forward to","correct":true,"rationale":"The phrase 'never start' stresses waiting without an end or reward, which creates a mood of hollow, endless waiting."},{"type":"x","text":"To show that the souls are being punished by monsters","correct":false,"rationale":"Students may assume every part of the Underworld involves monsters or torture, but the Fields of Asphodel are dangerous because of the souls' dull, uncaring existence, not attacks."},{"text":"To show that Hades is throwing a party for the souls","correct":false,"rationale":"This takes the concert literally. It is a figurative comparison, not an actual event."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners interpret figurative phrases by separating the literal picture from the idea it stands for.","sayAsk":"Say: 'A concert that will never start is a comparison. The souls are not at a concert.' Ask: 'What does the comparison show about how the souls spend their time?' Frames: 'The author compares ___ to ___.' 'This comparison shows that ___.' 'The mood is ___ because the words ___ suggest ___.' Allow students to sketch the literal picture first, then explain the meaning to a partner.","watchFor":"If students take the comparison literally, then prompt: 'Is the author describing a real concert? What is he really describing?' If students name the mood but give no evidence, then prompt: 'Which words in the text made you feel that way?' Success: the student names the two things compared and explains the feeling with a text detail."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: interpreting a comparison","tryThis":"Give students the frame '___ is like ___ because both ___.' Have them first draw each side of the comparison, then explain what they share."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: analyzing word choice","tryThis":"Ask students to find another modern image in pp. 300–309 and explain what Riordan gains by using it instead of an ancient one."}]}]},{"id":"lia-connotation-sort","title":"Part A2: Connotations of Waiting","minutes":8,"standards":["L.6.5.c","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 19","pages":"pp. 300–309"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Words can have the same basic meaning, or denotation, but different feelings, or connotations. *Wait*, *linger*, and *drift* all describe not doing much. But 'she waited' sounds neutral, 'she lingered' sounds like she doesn't want to leave, and 'she drifted' sounds aimless, like she has no direction. Authors pick the word with the right connotation."},{"type":"directions","text":"Think on your own for one minute, then share with a partner. Look at the words the author uses on these pages to describe how the souls move, speak, and look. Choose two and decide whether each has a positive, negative, or neutral connotation. Then think of a similar word with a different connotation and explain how it would change the feeling of the scene."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which word or phrase on these pages describes the souls, and what feeling does it carry?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The souls are described as drifting and waiting in a gray, quiet way. 'Drifting' feels negative to me because it means going nowhere with no purpose. If he said 'strolling' it would sound like they were enjoying themselves."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Now think about *wistfully*. How is it different from *sadly* or *angrily*?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Wistfully means sad but also longing, like missing something you can't have. Sadly is just sad, and angrily would mean they are mad. Wistfully fits the souls because they miss being alive but aren't fighting about it."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"If students struggle to find words on the pages, point them to the paragraphs describing the crowd. Accept any well-explained choice. The goal is explaining how connotation changes feeling, not finding one correct word."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners compare words with similar meanings but different feelings.","sayAsk":"Say: 'These words mean almost the same thing, but they feel different.' Ask: 'Which word feels more negative, and why?' Frames: 'The word ___ has a ___ connotation because ___.' 'If the author used ___ instead, the mood would feel ___.' Let students rate each word on a +/0/- line and discuss with a partner in any language before sharing in English.","watchFor":"If students give only dictionary definitions, then prompt: 'What feeling comes with the word, beyond its meaning?' If students pick positive and negative at random, then prompt: 'Would you want this word used to describe you?' Success: the student explains a difference in feeling between two similar words."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: connotation versus definition","tryThis":"Offer a word pair like thrifty and stingy. Ask 'Which would you want to be called?' to show that the feeling differs while the meaning is close. Then apply it to wait/linger/drift."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: precise word choice","tryThis":"Have students rank four words (wait, linger, drift, loiter) from most positive to most negative and justify the order, then revise one sentence from the text."}]}]},{"id":"lia-explain-danger-quick-write","title":"Part B: A Different Kind of Danger","minutes":14,"standards":["RL.6.4","L.6.5.c","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 19","pages":"pp. 300–309"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"This chapter shows an idea about justice. Some souls are rewarded, some are punished, and some are placed in the Fields of Asphodel because they did not do much good or much evil. Riordan uses modern comparisons to help us see that this is a kind of judgement too. Today we explain how his word choice shows that apathy, not caring, can be its own kind of danger."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How is the danger in the Fields of Asphodel different from the danger of a monster like the Minotaur or the Hydra?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A monster attacks you and you can fight it. In the Fields of Asphodel nothing attacks you, but you could be stuck forever not caring or doing anything. That is scarier in a way because there is nothing to fight."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What central idea about justice or punishment might this setting be showing?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It might show that not caring about right and wrong has consequences too. People who never did anything good or bad end up in a dull place with no purpose. So the story suggests that how you live matters, even if you never do anything terrible."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Model paragraph to display if needed: In Chapter 19, Rick Riordan uses figurative language to show that apathy is a different kind of danger than a monster. When he compares the souls to a crowd waiting for a concert that will never start, the phrase suggests endless waiting with no reward. This word choice creates a hollow, gloomy mood because the souls have nothing to hope for. As a result, the reader understands that the Fields of Asphodel are symbolic of a life spent not caring."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write a 4–5 sentence paragraph that answers: How does the apathy of the Fields of Asphodel represent a different kind of danger than a monster? Begin by naming the danger. Quote or closely paraphrase at least one figurative phrase from pp. 300–309. Explain what the phrase suggests using a connotation. Name the mood it creates. Use at least one vocabulary word (eternal, wistfully, apathy, symbolic, figurative, tragic, or judgement)."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Circulate and look for three things: (1) an actual phrase from the text, (2) an explanation of what it suggests, not just what it says, and (3) a named mood. Pull aside two or three strong examples to share in the Look Back if time allows."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in writing an evidence-based explanation that connects a figurative phrase to mood and idea.","sayAsk":"Say: 'First name the phrase, then explain what it suggests, then name the mood.' Ask: 'What does this phrase make the reader feel?' Frames: 'Riordan compares ___ to ___ to show ___.' 'The phrase ___ suggests ___, which creates a mood of ___.' 'This is a different kind of danger because ___.' Let students rehearse aloud with a partner, in a home language first if helpful, before writing.","watchFor":"If students retell the chapter, then prompt: 'Which phrase shows how Riordan wants us to feel?' If students list a quote without explaining it, then prompt: 'Add a sentence that begins This suggests...' Success: the student includes a text phrase, an explanation of its effect, and a mood word."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: connecting a phrase to mood","tryThis":"Provide a three-step frame: 'The author compares ___ to ___. This suggests ___. The mood is ___.' Allow students to say each sentence to a partner before writing it."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: linking to central ideas","tryThis":"Ask students to add a final sentence explaining what Riordan might be saying about justice or morality today, and to revise one word for a stronger connotation."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students synthesize the lesson by completing a sentence frame and reflecting on how figurative language shapes mood.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-exit-frame","title":"Figurative Language Exit Ticket","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.4"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"In the Performance Task, you will explain how an author's word choice shapes mood and ideas. Today you practiced that skill with the Fields of Asphodel."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the sentence frame on a sticky note or in your journal: 'Riordan's comparison of ___ to ___ creates a mood of ___ because ___. This shows that apathy is a different danger than a monster because ___.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which word or phrase from today changed the way you picture the Fields of Asphodel?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The concert that never starts changed it for me. I pictured a huge crowd just standing there bored forever, which feels sad and empty. It made me think that not caring could be as scary as a monster."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Collect the exit tickets. Sort them into 'names a phrase and a mood', 'names a phrase only', and 'retells', and use the sort to plan small groups for the next Flex Day."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (optional)","purpose":"Students read the next section of Chapter 19 to prepare for analyzing Hades's accusations and Percy's responses.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch19-next","title":"Read and Annotate pp. 310–319","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.1"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 19","pages":"pp. 310–319"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read and annotate pp. 310–319. As you read, underline one accusation Hades makes and one response Percy gives.
